items.purpose: The security-operations dashboard gives Kestrel's security and continuity leaders one trusted view of incidents, mean time to detect, contain and recover (MTTD, MTTC, MTTR), vulnerabilities by age, control results and restore performance. Sam Okafor (E-020), the Security Analyst, specifies it and builds it with Tomás Rivera (E-006); Daniel Osei (E-004), the Chief Information Security Officer, approves it. The Chief Information Officer, the Business Continuity Lead and the sponsor read it. You build it in week 11, day 5 (programme task 25, 2026-12-08 to 2026-12-11), and it is used at every weekly security meeting after Beacon closes. It joins PL-300 modelling and DAX with CISSP Security Operations and Security Assessment and Testing.

sections.heading: Purpose, audience and questions
sections.guidance: Name who uses the dashboard and the three or four questions it must answer, such as how long Kestrel takes to detect, contain and recover, and which vulnerabilities are past due. Every visual you add later must trace back to one of these questions. If a visual answers nothing on this list, leave it out.

sections.heading: Data sources and cleaning rules
sections.guidance: List the source files and every record that needs a data-quality rule, with its record ID and the rule (DQ-01, DQ-06 and so on). Good work keeps problem records visible: SEC-008 stays in incident counts even though it is left out of the time measures, and SEC-017 stays on the overdue list even though its score is wrong. Reconcile row counts: 21 source rows, 20 unique records, 10 incidents and 10 vulnerabilities.

sections.heading: Model design
sections.guidance: Describe each table, its grain (one row per what?) and its relationships. Keep a star: one-to-many, single direction, with dimensions filtering facts. Explain any table you deliberately do not relate, for example control tests that fall outside the date table's range. Say which columns are built in Power Query, such as the SequenceValid flag.

sections.heading: Measures (DAX)
sections.guidance: Give every measure its business definition, its DAX and the rows it leaves out on purpose. Write the exclusion into the measure (a filter on SequenceValid, a test for a blank recovery time) so nobody can forget it. Use DIVIDE for ratios and a fixed as-of date while testing, so expected values do not change from day to day.

sections.heading: Tested values
sections.guidance: Put each measure next to its expected value from truth.json, the number of rows behind it, and the wrong value you get if a cleaning rule is skipped. This is your test evidence. A measure without a reconciled expected value is not ready to publish.

sections.heading: Pages and visuals
sections.guidance: Lay out one page per question group: incidents and response times, vulnerabilities, control health and restores. Show the count behind every average, draw targets as reference lines, and never rely on colour alone. Add alt text and check the tab order so the pages work with a screen reader.

sections.heading: Security, refresh and ownership
sections.guidance: Say which workspace holds the report, who gets which workspace role, which sensitivity label applies, how often it refreshes and whether a gateway is needed. Name the owner of the measures and the owner of the definitions, and when they review them. Explain why row-level security (RLS) is or is not needed: it filters data only for Viewers.

items.modelDocument:
- Document ID: BCN-R3-09
- Title: Security-operations dashboard specification
- Owner: Sam Okafor (E-020), Security Analyst
- Approver: Daniel Osei (E-004), Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)
- Version: 1.0
- Date: 2026-12-11
- Status: Approved
- Data: khn_security_events.csv and khn_controls.csv, extract as of 2026-10-01

## Purpose, audience and questions

Audience: the CISO, Marcus Bell (E-002, Chief Information Officer) and Chloe Dubois (E-016, Business Continuity Lead). Questions:

1. How long do we take to detect, contain and recover: mean time to detect (MTTD), contain (MTTC) and recover (MTTR)?
2. Which open vulnerabilities are past their remediation due date?
3. Which controls fail, and do restores of the Clinical Information System (CIS) and other tier 1 systems meet each recovery time objective (RTO)?

## Data sources and cleaning rules

| Record | Problem | Handling |
|---|---|---|
| SEC-005 | Exact duplicate row | DQ-01: remove the copy; 21 rows become 20 |
| SEC-008 | Contained before detected | DQ-06: kept in counts; SequenceValid = false, so out of MTTD, MTTC and MTTR |
| SEC-009 | Not yet recovered | Out of MTTR only |
| SEC-017 | Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score 11.5 | DQ-05: score nulled; kept in open and overdue counts |
| SEC-016 | Asset A-021 not registered | DQ-10: Unknown asset |
| SEC-019 | Severity "hIGH" | DQ-03: mapped to High |

## Model design

- Power Query renames the source columns to the names used below (record_type to RecordType, occurred_at to OccurredAt, remediation_due to RemediationDue, restore_hours to RestoreHours, rto_target_hours to RTOTargetHours, and so on) and sets the timestamp columns to Date/Time, so blank times load as null.
- FactSecurityEvent: one row per security record (10 incidents, 10 vulnerabilities). Power Query adds SequenceValid as a True/False column with this step, typed logical so the DAX test against TRUE () works:

```
= Table.AddColumn(
    #"Renamed Columns",
    "SequenceValid",
    each [RecordType] = "Incident"
        and [OccurredAt] <= [DetectedAt]
        and [DetectedAt] <= [ContainedAt]
        and ([RecoveredAt] = null or [ContainedAt] <= [RecoveredAt]),
    type logical
)
```

- FactControlTest: one row per control test (13). Not related to DimDate: restore tests go back to 2025, and DimDate covers only 2026 (2026-01-01 to 2026-12-31).
- DimAsset (15 systems plus Unknown) filters both facts, one to many, single direction.

## Measures (DAX)

```
As Of Date = DATE ( 2026, 10, 1 )

Incidents =
CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( FactSecurityEvent ), FactSecurityEvent[RecordType] = "Incident" )

MTTD Hours =
AVERAGEX (
    FILTER ( FactSecurityEvent, FactSecurityEvent[SequenceValid] = TRUE () ),
    DATEDIFF ( FactSecurityEvent[OccurredAt], FactSecurityEvent[DetectedAt], MINUTE ) / 60
)

MTTC Hours =
AVERAGEX (
    FILTER ( FactSecurityEvent, FactSecurityEvent[SequenceValid] = TRUE () ),
    DATEDIFF ( FactSecurityEvent[DetectedAt], FactSecurityEvent[ContainedAt], MINUTE ) / 60
)

MTTR Hours =
AVERAGEX (
    FILTER (
        FactSecurityEvent,
        FactSecurityEvent[SequenceValid] = TRUE ()
            && NOT ISBLANK ( FactSecurityEvent[RecoveredAt] )
    ),
    DATEDIFF ( FactSecurityEvent[DetectedAt], FactSecurityEvent[RecoveredAt], MINUTE ) / 60
)

Open Vulnerabilities =
CALCULATE (
    COUNTROWS ( FactSecurityEvent ),
    FactSecurityEvent[RecordType] = "Vulnerability",
    FactSecurityEvent[Status] = "Open"
)

Overdue Vulnerabilities =
VAR AsOf = [As Of Date]
RETURN
    CALCULATE ( [Open Vulnerabilities], FactSecurityEvent[RemediationDue] < AsOf )

Controls Passing % =
DIVIDE (
    CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( FactControlTest ), FactControlTest[Status] = "Pass" ),
    COUNTROWS ( FactControlTest )
)

Restore Tests Within RTO =
COUNTROWS (
    FILTER (
        FactControlTest,
        NOT ISBLANK ( FactControlTest[RestoreHours] )
            && FactControlTest[RestoreHours] <= FactControlTest[RTOTargetHours]
    )
)

Days Since Last CIS Restore Test =
DATEDIFF (
    CALCULATE ( MAX ( FactControlTest[RestoreTestDate] ), FactControlTest[AssetID] = "A-001" ),
    [As Of Date],
    DAY
)
```

SequenceValid is false for every vulnerability, so the three time measures only ever see valid incidents.

## Tested values

| Measure | Expected | Rows used | Wrong value if a rule is skipped |
|---|---|---|---|
| Incidents | 10 | 10 unique | 11 with the SEC-005 copy |
| MTTD Hours | 25.29 | 9 | 24.23 with the SEC-005 copy; 23.11 with SEC-008 |
| MTTC Hours | 1.93 | 9 | 1.82 with the copy; 1.60 with SEC-008 |
| MTTR Hours | 28.33 | 8 (no SEC-009) | 25.55 with the copy; 27.24 with SEC-008 |
| Open Vulnerabilities | 8 | includes SEC-017 | 7 if SEC-017 is dropped |
| Overdue Vulnerabilities | 3 | SEC-012, SEC-015, SEC-017 | 2 if SEC-017 is dropped |
| Controls Passing % | 30.8% | 4 of 13 | 33.3% if Not tested is left out |
| Restore Tests Within RTO | 1 | CT-003 of 3 run | |
| Days Since Last CIS Restore Test | 413 | CT-002, 2025-08-14 | |

Incidents by severity: Critical 1, High 3, Medium 4, Low 2.

## Pages and visuals

1. Incidents: MTTD, MTTC and MTTR cards with the incident count beside each; incidents by severity; a table with SequenceValid shown so SEC-008 stays visible.
2. Vulnerabilities: open by severity and age band (0-30 days 6, 31-60 days 1, over 60 days 1); overdue table with SEC-017 marked "rescore".
3. Controls and restores: restore hours against RTO with a target line; training by group against 90%.

## Security, refresh and ownership

- Workspace "Beacon Security Operations": Sam Okafor Member; the CISO, the Chief Information Officer and the Business Continuity Lead get app access or the Viewer role, so they can read but not edit.
- Sensitivity label Confidential. No patient data, and every viewer may see every record, so no row-level security (RLS) roles.
- Daily refresh (proposed); a gateway only if the extract sits on an on-premises share. At go-live, As Of Date becomes TODAY ().
- Measures: Sam Okafor. Definitions: Daniel Osei. Reviewed monthly.
mistakes: Averaging over every incident row, so the SEC-005 copy counts twice and SEC-008's negative containment time is included: MTTC falls to 1.54 hours instead of 1.93 (1.60 from SEC-008 alone).
Dropping SEC-017 because its CVSS score is impossible, which hides a Critical vulnerability that is past due.
Testing with TODAY () instead of a fixed as-of date, so the expected values change every day and cannot be reconciled.
Showing an average with no count beside it: with only 8 or 9 incidents, one long recovery moves MTTR a lot.

items.purpose: The business impact analysis (BIA) shows how harm to patients and to Kestrel grows, hour by hour, when a clinical service stops, and turns that into a ranked list of services with an agreed maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) for each. Chloe Dubois (E-016), the Business Continuity Lead, writes it with the business owners; Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001) approves it. You build it in week 12, day 1 (programme task 21, 2026-11-27 to 2026-12-03). The RTO and RPO recommendation, the disaster-recovery and downtime plan and the tabletop exercise all start from it. It practises CISSP Security and Risk Management (business continuity requirements), PMP value and priorities, and ITIL service continuity.

sections.heading: Scope, method and approval
sections.guidance: State which services and sites are in scope, how you gathered the evidence (workshop, interviews, the Beacon data), who took part and who approved the result. Say plainly that a BIA measures impact if a service stops; it does not rate likelihood, which belongs in the risk register.

sections.heading: Impact scale
sections.guidance: Define a rating scale with plain descriptions for each impact category: patient safety, operational, financial, and legal and regulatory. Two people rating the same outage should land on the same number. Name the Health Information Act duty correctly if you use it in the legal row.

sections.heading: Clinical services and dependencies
sections.guidance: List clinical services, not systems, each with its business owner, then the systems each one needs. Look for hidden dependencies: almost every clinical system signs in through the Identity Directory (A-007), and every restore needs the Backup Platform (A-012). Flag any service whose owner is missing.

sections.heading: Impact over time
sections.guidance: Rate each service at fixed time points such as 1, 4, 8, 24 and 72 hours, and show the evidence behind the ratings. Use proportions from the data (occupancy, share of ambulance arrivals, length of stay) rather than invented volumes. Impact should rise over time; a flat row usually means nobody thought about it.

sections.heading: Maximum tolerable downtime and ranking
sections.guidance: Set an MTD for each service at or before the first time point rated Severe, and rank services by MTD, then by impact. Show the current recovery time objective (RTO) of each supporting system next to it so mismatches stand out. MTD is a business decision, recorded as agreed, not a number IT picks.

sections.heading: Data-loss tolerance
sections.guidance: Ask each owner how much recent data the service could lose and rebuild, measured in time, and how it would be rebuilt (paper records, census sheets, reload from source). Record the work recovery time needed after a restore. These answers become the recovery point objective (RPO) and work recovery time (WRT) inputs for the next document.

sections.heading: Findings and next steps
sections.guidance: List the gaps the analysis exposed, each with the evidence and who must act, then name the documents and tests that use the BIA next. Good findings are specific: a record ID, a date, a measured value against the target.

items.modelDocument:
- Document ID: BCN-R3-10
- Title: Business impact analysis for clinical services
- Owner: Chloe Dubois (E-016), Business Continuity Lead
- Approver: Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), VP Clinical Operations and executive sponsor
- Version: 1.0
- Date: 2026-12-03
- Status: Approved
- Figures: data as of 2026-10-01; ratings, maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) and work recovery time (WRT) agreed at the workshop on 2026-12-01

## Scope, method and approval

Scope: clinical services at Kestrel General Hospital (KGH), Aspen Ridge (ARH), Coulee Valley (CVH) and Prairie Gate (PGH) that depend on the 15 systems in the critical clinical system inventory. Method: one workshop with each business owner, follow-up interviews, and the Beacon baseline data (2026-07-01 to 2026-09-30). This analysis rates impact if a service stops, not likelihood. Approved by Dr. Helen Marchetti on 2026-12-03.

## Impact scale

Ratings 1 Minimal to 5 Severe. A service's rating at each time point is its highest category.

| Category | 3 Moderate | 5 Severe |
|---|---|---|
| Patient safety | Delays in care, no harm expected | Harm likely: missed results, medication errors |
| Operational | Paper workarounds slow work | Units cannot admit, discharge or transfer safely |
| Financial | Overtime within budget | Unbudgeted recovery spend needing executive approval |
| Legal and regulatory | Records need back-entry | Health Information Act duties at risk: safeguards (section 60) or breach notification (section 60.1) |

## Clinical services and dependencies

| Service | Business owner | Systems needed |
|---|---|---|
| S1 Clinical communication | E-001 | A-014 Clinical Paging, A-007 |
| S2 Emergency care | E-007 | A-002 Emergency Department Tracking Board, A-001 Clinical Information System (CIS), A-003, A-004, A-008, A-007 |
| S3 Inpatient care and medication | E-001; Pharmacy owner not named | A-001, A-005 Pharmacy System, A-008, A-007 |
| S4 Laboratory testing | E-001 | A-003, A-001, A-007 |
| S5 Patient flow | E-008 | A-006 Bed Management, A-001, A-007 |
| S6 Diagnostic imaging | E-001 | A-004 Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS), A-007 |
| S7 Patient-flow analytics | E-008 | A-009, A-010 |

Twelve systems sign in through the Identity Directory (A-007). Clinicians at shared workstations reach the CIS through the Virtual Desktop Service (A-008). Every restore needs the Backup Platform (A-012), which is missing from depends_on in khn_assets.csv.

## Impact over time

Evidence: 121 of 144 staffed beds occupied on 2026-09-30 and 87.0% average daily occupancy; 23.2% of 474 emergency department (ED) visits arrived by ambulance and 11.2% were Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS) level 1 or 2 (computed from khn_ed_visits.csv); admitted ED patients stayed a median 11.96 hours, so an outage at any hour hits patients already in the department.

| Service | 1 h | 4 h | 8 h | 24 h | 72 h |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 Clinical communication | 4 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 |
| S2 Emergency care | 3 | 4 | 5 | 5 | 5 |
| S3 Inpatient care and medication | 3 | 4 | 5 | 5 | 5 |
| S4 Laboratory testing | 3 | 4 | 5 | 5 | 5 |
| S5 Patient flow | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| S6 Diagnostic imaging | 2 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 |
| S7 Patient-flow analytics | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 |

## Maximum tolerable downtime and ranking

Each MTD sits at or before the first time point rated 5. Ties are ranked by the owners. The last column is each system's current recovery time objective (RTO) from khn_assets.csv.

| Rank | Service | MTD (agreed) | Current RTO of its systems |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | S1 Clinical communication | 4 h | A-014 2 h; A-007 2 h |
| 2 | S2 Emergency care | 8 h | A-001, A-002, A-003, A-008 4 h; A-004 24 h |
| 3 | S3 Inpatient care and medication | 8 h | A-001, A-005, A-008 4 h |
| 4 | S4 Laboratory testing | 8 h | A-003 4 h |
| 5 | S5 Patient flow | 24 h | A-006 8 h |
| 6 | S6 Diagnostic imaging | 48 h | A-004 24 h |
| 7 | S7 Patient-flow analytics | 120 h | A-009 72 h; A-010 24 h |

## Data-loss tolerance

- S1 to S4: up to 1 hour, rebuilt from paper downtime records (matches the 1-hour recovery point objective, RPO, of A-001, A-002, A-003, A-005, A-014).
- WRT (agreed) after a restore: 2 h for the CIS, Pharmacy (A-005) and Laboratory (A-003); 1 h for the ED Tracking Board (A-002) and Virtual Desktop Service (A-008); 0.5 h for the Identity Directory (A-007), Clinical Paging (A-014) and Backup Platform (A-012).
- S5: up to 4 hours, rebuilt from unit census sheets. S7: up to 24 hours, reloaded from source.

## Findings and next steps

1. The CIS failed two restore tests (9.0 h and 13.5 h, last on 2025-08-14), far beyond the 8-hour MTD of S2 and S3 (risk R-04).
2. A-005 Pharmacy System has no business owner and has never been restore-tested (CT-004).
3. A-014, needed by the top-ranked service, passed end of support on 2026-06-30.
4. A-004's 24-hour RTO exceeds the 8-hour MTD of S2; agreed workaround: read images at the scanner consoles.
5. The restore tests use daily backup jobs, which alone cannot meet a 1-hour RPO.

Next: the RTO and RPO recommendation (2026-12-03) and the CIS restore test in task 22 (2026-12-04 to 2026-12-11).
mistakes: Rating likelihood instead of impact: a BIA asks what happens if the service stops, not how likely that is.
Listing systems instead of clinical services, so recovery order follows the IT structure rather than harm to patients.
Letting IT set the MTD. It is a business decision made by the owners who carry the consequences.
Missing hidden dependencies such as the Identity Directory and the Backup Platform, which must be working before anything else can be restored.

items.purpose: The RTO and RPO recommendation sets, for each tier 1 system, how fast it must be restored (recovery time objective, RTO) and how much recent data Kestrel can afford to lose (recovery point objective, RPO). It checks every target against the maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) and work recovery time from the business impact analysis (BIA), and compares it with real restore evidence. Daniel Osei (E-004) writes it with Chloe Dubois (E-016) right after the BIA; each system's business owner approves its own targets, and Marcus Bell (E-002) commits IT to meet them. You build it in week 12, day 2. The disaster-recovery plan, the control-testing plan and the Clinical Information System (CIS) restore test in programme task 22 all use it. CISSP Security Operations (recovery strategies) and Security and Risk Management (business continuity requirements).

sections.heading: Decision requested
sections.guidance: Open with the decision you need and your recommendation in two or three sentences. Here the hard question is whether to keep the 4-hour CIS RTO that two restore tests failed. A reader who stops after this section should still know what you advise and why.

sections.heading: Rules and inputs
sections.guidance: State the rules you apply: RTO plus work recovery time (WRT) must not exceed the MTD, and the RPO cannot be shorter than the gap between recoverable copies. Name each input and where it came from: MTD and WRT from the BIA (agreed), targets from khn_assets.csv, tests from khn_controls.csv.

sections.heading: Recommended targets
sections.guidance: Give one row per tier 1 system with MTD, RTO, WRT, the RTO plus WRT check and the RPO. Label every value as data, agreed or proposed. Show the arithmetic so a reviewer can check each row against the rule without asking you.

sections.heading: Restore evidence against targets
sections.guidance: Put every restore test and real recovery next to its target: date, measured hours, pass or fail and the reason recorded. Say which tier 1 systems have no test at all. Check the RPO too: a daily backup job cannot deliver a 1-hour RPO on its own.

sections.heading: Dependencies and recovery chain
sections.guidance: Work out what must be restored first and add up the chain. A target can pass on its own and still fail once you add the system it waits for. Look at the Identity Directory, the Virtual Desktop Service and the Backup Platform.

sections.heading: Gap closure actions
sections.guidance: For every gap between target and evidence, give one action with an owner and a date. Fix the capability; do not move the target to match a failed test. Tie actions to the findings recorded in the tests, such as the out-of-date runbook.

sections.heading: Approval
sections.guidance: Record which business owner approved each system's targets and on what date. A target with no owner is a proposal, not a business-approved objective, so say so. Note which risk stays open and who owns it.

items.modelDocument:
- Document ID: BCN-R3-11
- Title: Recovery time objective (RTO) and recovery point objective (RPO) recommendation, tier 1 systems
- Owner: Daniel Osei (E-004), Chief Information Security Officer
- Contributor: Chloe Dubois (E-016), Business Continuity Lead
- Approvers: each system's business owner; Marcus Bell (E-002), Chief Information Officer, for IT delivery
- Version: 1.0
- Date: 2026-12-03
- Status: Approved except A-005

## Decision requested

Confirm recovery targets for the eight tier 1 systems and decide whether to keep the 4-hour RTO for the Clinical Information System (CIS, A-001) that two restore tests failed. Recommendation: keep it. Moving it to the measured 13.5 hours would break the 8-hour maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) agreed in the business impact analysis (BIA).

## Rules and inputs

- RTO plus work recovery time (WRT) must not exceed the MTD. CIS: 4 h + 2 h = 6 h, inside 8 h. A 12-hour RTO would give 14 h and fail.
- The RPO cannot be shorter than the gap between recoverable copies.
- Inputs: MTD and WRT from the BIA (agreed at the 2026-12-01 workshop, approved 2026-12-03); targets from khn_assets.csv; tests from khn_controls.csv; the SEC-004 recovery from khn_security_events.csv.

## Recommended targets

| System | MTD (agreed) | RTO | WRT (agreed) | RTO + WRT | RPO |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A-001 CIS | 8 h | 4 h | 2 h | 6 h | 1 h |
| A-002 Emergency Department Tracking Board | 8 h | 4 h | 1 h | 5 h | 1 h |
| A-003 Laboratory Information System | 8 h | 4 h | 2 h | 6 h | 1 h |
| A-005 Pharmacy System | 8 h | 4 h (proposed) | 2 h | 6 h | 1 h |
| A-007 Identity Directory | 4 h | 2 h | 0.5 h | 2.5 h | 1 h |
| A-008 Virtual Desktop Service | 8 h | 4 h | 1 h | 5 h | 24 h |
| A-012 Backup Platform | Supports every restore | 2 h (proposed; now 8 h) | 0.5 h | 2.5 h | 24 h |
| A-014 Clinical Paging | 4 h | 2 h | 0.5 h | 2.5 h | 1 h |

Every row passes on paper. Tier 2 and tier 3 targets stay as in khn_assets.csv.

## Restore evidence against targets

| System | Evidence | Measured | Target | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A-001 | CT-001, 2025-03-20: database rebuild step ran long | 9.0 h | 4 h | Fail |
| A-001 | CT-002, 2025-08-14: restore runbook out of date | 13.5 h | 4 h | Fail |
| A-007 | CT-003, 2026-09-10 | 1.5 h | 2 h | Pass |
| A-005 | CT-004 | Never run | 4 h | Not tested |
| A-008 | SEC-004, detection to normal service | 63.42 h | 4 h | Fail (real incident) |

No restore test is on file for A-002, A-003, A-008, A-012 or A-014. The last CIS test was 413 days before 2026-10-01. At the measured 13.5 h, the CIS needs 13.5 + 2 = 15.5 h, nearly twice its MTD.

RPO: the tests used daily jobs (BK-A001-DAILY, BK-A005-DAILY, BK-A007-DAILY). A daily copy alone allows up to 24 hours of loss, so the 1-hour RPO holds only if transaction logs are copied at least hourly. That is not yet evidenced.

## Dependencies and recovery chain

The CIS needs A-007 for sign-in. If both are hit and you restore them one after the other: 2 h + 4 h + 2 h WRT = 8 h, exactly the MTD, with no margin. So the CIS database restore must start in parallel with A-007. The Backup Platform (A-012) must work before any restore starts; its current 8-hour RTO cannot support a 4-hour CIS RTO. Proposed: 2 h, backed by the immutable copy confirmed in CT-005 (2026-09-24).

## Gap closure actions

| Action | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|
| Rewrite the CIS runbook and fix the database rebuild step | Kevin Park (E-009) with Raj Patel (E-015, Meridian Clinical Systems) | 2026-12-04 |
| Timed CIS restore into an isolated environment (task 22) | Chloe Dubois (E-016) | 2026-12-11 |
| Prove hourly log copies for A-001, A-005, A-007 | Kevin Park (E-009) | 2026-12-11 |
| Name a Pharmacy System owner, then test its restore | Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001) | 2026-12-11 |
| Add A-002, A-003, A-008, A-012, A-014 to the 2027 restore-test calendar | Chloe Dubois (E-016) | 2027-01-29 |

## Approval

| Systems | Approver | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| A-001, A-003, A-014 | Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001) | Approved 2026-12-03 |
| A-002 | Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007) | Approved 2026-12-03 |
| A-007, A-008, A-012 | Marcus Bell (E-002) | Approved, including A-012 at 2 h |
| A-005 | No business owner | Not approved: stays proposed |

Risk R-04 stays open with Daniel Osei (E-004) until two consecutive CIS restore tests pass within 4 hours (agreed).
mistakes: Moving the RTO to match a failed test. The target comes from the MTD the business can tolerate, not from what IT manages today.
Leaving out work recovery time, so RTO equals MTD and there is no time to back-enter the paper records.
Promising a 1-hour RPO when the only backup evidenced runs once a day.
Setting targets system by system without adding up the recovery chain through the Identity Directory and the Backup Platform.

items.purpose: The control-testing plan says how Kestrel will prove that its key security and continuity controls work. For each control it names the population, the sample, the evidence, the expected result, the tester and what happens when a test fails. Daniel Osei (E-004) owns it, testers who do not operate the controls run it, and Marcus Bell (E-002) approves it. You build it in week 12, day 2, next to the RTO and RPO recommendation; it is dated 2026-12-04, the start of programme task 22, and drives the December restore tests and the quarterly testing after Beacon. CISSP Security Assessment and Testing.

sections.heading: Scope and objectives
sections.guidance: List the controls in scope and the question each test answers: does the control operate as designed, every time, over the period? Choose the controls that carry Beacon's promises on recovery, access and privacy rather than every control Kestrel has.

sections.heading: Test approach and sampling
sections.guidance: Explain test of design and test of operating effectiveness, when you test the whole population and when you sample, how samples are picked, and the independence rule. Label any sample sizes as Kestrel's own guide. Say what one exception means for the result.

sections.heading: Key controls to test
sections.guidance: One row per control: ID, control, population and sample, evidence, and expected result. The expected result must be written before the test and must be measurable, for example restored in 4 hours or less with data no older than 1 hour.

sections.heading: Baseline results
sections.guidance: Record what the last tests found, straight from khn_controls.csv and the reconciled data, with IDs and values. The baseline shows where retesting matters most and gives the dashboard its starting point.

sections.heading: Schedule and testers
sections.guidance: Give each test a tester and a date. Check independence: the tester must not operate the control. Restore tests need an operator who runs the restore and a separate witness who times and records it.

sections.heading: Deficiencies and remediation

- Document ID: BCN-R3-12
- Title: Control-testing plan, Release 3 and 2027
- Owner: Daniel Osei (E-004), Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)
- Approver: Marcus Bell (E-002), Chief Information Officer (CIO)
- Version: 1.0
- Date: 2026-12-04
- Status: Approved

## Scope and objectives

Tests the controls behind Beacon's recovery, access and privacy promises: restores of tier 1 systems, immutable backups, multi-factor authentication (MFA) for privileged accounts, leaver removal, access reviews, segregation of duties (SoD), vulnerability remediation and awareness training. Each test answers one question: does the control operate as designed, every time, over the period?

## Test approach and sampling

- Test of design first: walk one item through and read the procedure. Then test operating effectiveness over the period.
- Where a query can check every item, test the whole population. Kestrel's identity and vulnerability data is small enough for this.
- Manual controls (Kestrel sampling guide, proposed): daily 25 items, weekly 5, monthly 2, picked at random with the seed recorded.
- A tester never tests a control they operate. Kevin Park (E-009) runs provisioning and backups, so he cannot test them.
- One exception fails the test. It is investigated, not averaged away.

## Key controls to test

| ID | Control | Population and sample | Evidence | Expected result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CT-014 | Clinical Information System (CIS) restore (A-001) | Latest BK-A001-DAILY copy; 1 timed full restore to an isolated environment | Timed runbook log; clinician data check | 4 h or less; data no older than 1 h |
| CT-015 | Pharmacy System restore (A-005) | Latest BK-A005-DAILY copy; 1 full restore | Timed runbook log | 4 h or less |
| CT-005 | Immutable backup copy (A-012) | Tier 1 copies for November 2026; configuration once plus 5 random days | NorthArc Cloud (V-02) console export | Immutable copy in a Canadian region on every day sampled |
| CT-006 | MFA for privileged accounts | All enabled privileged accounts, plus E-031 (flag "Maybe") | Identity Directory export | 100% enrolled |
| CT-008 | Leaver accounts disabled | Every worker terminated or past end date | HR and Payroll System (A-015) matched to A-007 | No enabled leaver |
| CT-007 | Quarterly access reviews | Every review due in the quarter | Dated review records | 100% done, decisions carried out |
| CT-016 | SoD on A-007 | Every A-007 permission row | Permission export | Nobody holds two of: provision, approve, administer audit logs |
| CT-017 | Vulnerability remediation | Every vulnerability detected in the quarter | Scanner and ticket records | Fixed within 7, 30, 60 or 90 days by severity |
| CT-009 to CT-013 | Awareness training | All five workforce groups | Training records | 90% or more in each group |

## Baseline results

From khn_controls.csv and the Beacon data as of 2026-10-01: 4 Pass, 8 Fail, 1 Not tested of 13 tests.

- CIS restore failed twice (9.0 h and 13.5 h against 4 h); Identity Directory passed (1.5 h against 2 h); Pharmacy never tested.
- Immutable copy passed on 2026-09-24.
- Privileged MFA 4 of 6 (66.7%); E-009 and E-015 not enrolled.
- Leavers E-014 and E-027 still enabled (population of 3 with E-042).
- Access reviews 12 of 18 due (66.7%); 6 overdue.
- SoD: E-009 holds all three duties.
- Vulnerabilities: 3 of 8 open are past due (SEC-012, SEC-015, SEC-017).
- Training below 90%: agency and vendor workers 48%, physicians 71%, nursing 86%.

## Schedule and testers

| Tests | Operator | Tester | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| CT-014, CT-015 | Kevin Park (E-009), Raj Patel (E-015) | Chloe Dubois (E-016) times and witnesses | 2026-12-04 to 2026-12-11 (task 22) |
| CT-005, CT-006, CT-007, CT-008, CT-016 | Kevin Park, Grace Liu (E-005) | Sam Okafor (E-020) | 2026-12-07 to 2026-12-11, then quarterly |
| CT-017 | Sam Okafor (E-020) | Daniel Osei (E-004) | Quarterly from January 2027 |
| CT-009 to CT-013 | Nora Lindqvist (E-018) | Sam Okafor (E-020) | Quarterly from January 2027 |

## Deficiencies and remediation

- A failure is Significant if it affects a tier 1 system or patient data, otherwise Minor. Significant items go to the residual risk register.
- The control owner raises a remediation item within 5 working days, with an owner and due date.
- A control passes only when its retest passes.
- Known from the baseline: the CIS runbook and database rebuild step (E-009 with V-01); MFA for E-009 and E-015; disable E-014 and E-027 and find why the leaver events did not reach IT (E-018); remove approve and audit-log rights from E-009; a training plan with ClearPath Staffing (V-03).

## Reporting and sign-off

Results are recorded one row per test in the khn_controls.csv format (Pass, Fail or Not tested), so the security-operations dashboard shows them at the next refresh. Daniel Osei signs each result; Marcus Bell approves the plan and receives a quarterly summary.
mistakes: Accepting a backup job's success message as proof of recovery. Only a timed restore shows whether the RTO can be met.
Letting the person who operates a control test it, for example Kevin Park testing the provisioning he performs.
Sampling when a query can check the whole population, or explaining away a single exception.
Writing the expected result after the test, so any outcome can be called a pass.

sections.guidance: Say which systems and clinical areas the plan covers and give clear activation triggers that someone can apply at 3 a.m. Name who declares a disaster and who stands in. Make clear that units start downtime procedures straight away and do not wait for a declaration.

items.modelDocument:
- Document ID: BCN-R3-13
- Title: Disaster-recovery (DR) and downtime plan for clinical systems
- Owner: Chloe Dubois (E-016), Business Continuity Lead
- Approvers: Marcus Bell (E-002), Chief Information Officer (CIO); Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), executive sponsor
- Version: 1.0
- Date: 2026-12-11
- Status: Approved
- Targets: recovery time objectives (RTO) and work recovery times (WRT) from BCN-R3-11; maximum tolerable downtimes (MTD) from the business impact analysis (BIA), BCN-R3-10

## Scope and activation

Covers the eight tier 1 systems and every clinical area at the four sites (KGH, ARH, CVH and PGH). Activate when any of these is true:

- a tier 1 system is down and the technical lead expects recovery to take longer than its RTO;
- ransomware or other destructive malware is confirmed on a clinical system;
- two or more tier 1 systems are down at once.

Marcus Bell declares a disaster, or Daniel Osei (E-004) if he cannot be reached within 15 minutes. Units start downtime procedures at once and do not wait for the declaration.

## Roles and contacts

| Role | Person | Duty |
|---|---|---|
| Declaration | Marcus Bell (E-002) | Declares, approves spending, briefs the executive |
| Recovery coordinator | Chloe Dubois (E-016) | Runs the plan, keeps the log, reports every hour |
| Security lead | Daniel Osei (E-004), Sam Okafor (E-020) | Contains the attack; confirms the restore point is clean |
| Technical lead | Kevin Park (E-009), Ahmed Haddad (E-017) | Restores systems and network |
| Vendor support | Raj Patel (E-015), Meridian Clinical Systems | Clinical Information System (CIS) database and application |
| Clinical lead | Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007) and unit managers | Downtime procedures and safety decisions |
| Privacy | Priya Raman (E-003) | Breach assessment under the Health Information Act |
| Service desk | Grace Liu (E-005) | Major incident record and staff updates |

## Recovery order

| Step | Systems | RTO | Restore from |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A-012 Backup Platform check; A-007 Identity Directory; CIS database restore starts in parallel | 2 h | Immutable copy at NorthArc Cloud (V-02); BK-A007-DAILY |
| 2 | A-014 Clinical Paging; A-001 CIS; A-008 Virtual Desktop Service | 2 h; 4 h; 4 h | Clean backups; A-008 from clean images |
| 3 | A-002, A-003, A-005 | 4 h | Own backups, after A-001 |
| 4 | Tier 2, then tier 3 | 8 h to 72 h | khn_assets.csv targets |

Restore only from a copy the security lead has confirmed clean. Rebuild on clean servers; never clean an infected one and put it back.

## CIS recovery runbook

Time budget from the declaration (proposed, proven or corrected in task 22):

1. 0:00 to 0:30: isolate the affected zones; Sam Okafor and Sentinel SOC Services (V-04) confirm the last clean restore point; Raj Patel joins.
2. 0:30 to 1:00: prepare clean servers in the recovery zone; start the restore of the latest immutable BK-A001-DAILY copy.
3. 1:00 to 2:30: restore the database and apply transaction logs to the clean point (recovery point objective, RPO, of 1 h), using the rewritten rebuild step.
4. 2:30 to 3:15: restore the application tier and connect it to A-007.
5. 3:15 to 3:45: check interfaces to A-002, A-003 and A-005 and compare record counts with the last downtime report.
6. 3:45 to 4:00: two named clinicians check sample records; the coordinator declares the CIS available.

Every step is timed in the log. A step 15 minutes over budget is escalated to Marcus Bell.

## Clinical downtime procedures

- All areas: paper forms from the unit downtime box, and the downtime report workstation on each unit (current patients, allergies and active orders, refreshed every hour, proposed).
- Emergency department: paper triage with the Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS) level, a whiteboard in place of A-002, paper lab and imaging requests, critical results phoned to the charge nurse (Aisha Mahmoud, E-010, at KGH).
- Inpatient units: paper medication administration record (MAR) from the last downtime report; pharmacy confirms new orders by phone.
- Laboratory: hand-labelled samples and a paper log.
- Paging down: overhead calls and the unit phone tree.
- Unit clerks, such as Ben Kowalski (E-011) on Medicine 4A, keep every paper record for back-entry.

## Return to normal operations

1. The coordinator confirms each system is clean, restored and checked by its clinical lead.
2. Units back-enter paper records within the agreed WRT (2 h for the CIS), so RTO plus WRT stays inside the 8-hour MTD.
3. Unit clerks confirm every paper record is entered; pharmacy confirms every downtime medication is recorded.
4. The clinical lead approves the return to the system; the paper records stay part of the health record.
5. Priya Raman completes the risk-of-harm assessment. If there is a risk of harm, Kestrel notifies the Information and Privacy Commissioner, the Minister responsible under the Act and the affected individuals (Health Information Act, section 60.1).
6. A post-incident review follows within 10 working days (proposed).

## Testing and maintenance

- Test types, least to most disruptive: read-through, tabletop walk-through, simulation, parallel test, full interruption.
- The CIS gets a timed technical restore into an isolated environment that does not touch production (task 22, 2026-12-04 to 2026-12-11). It is not a full parallel test, because the restored system processes no live work.
- Calendar (proposed): CIS restore twice a year, every other tier 1 system once a year, one tabletop a year.
- Update the plan after every test, real incident or system change; check the contact list every quarter.
mistakes: Restoring onto infected servers, or from a backup nobody has confirmed clean, so the attacker comes back with the data.
Recovery steps with no names, no time budget and no order based on dependencies.
Downtime procedures written by IT alone that clinical units have never seen or practised.
No return-to-normal section, so paper records from the downtime never reach the CIS and the health record is incomplete.

items.purpose: The tabletop-exercise scenario is the script for a discussion-based exercise in which Kestrel's leaders talk through a ransomware attack step by step, so that gaps in decisions, roles and assumptions show up in a meeting room instead of during a real outage. Daniel Osei (E-004) owns it, Chloe Dubois (E-016) designs and facilitates it, and Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001) approves the objectives. You build it in week 12, day 3, together with the disaster-recovery plan; the exercise runs in programme task 23 (2026-12-04 to 2026-12-10), and its findings update the ransomware playbook, the escalation and breach-notification matrix and the disaster-recovery and downtime plan. CISSP Security Operations (business continuity planning and exercises) and the PMP task Engage stakeholders.

sections.heading: Purpose and objectives
sections.guidance: Write three to five objectives that can be observed in the room, each tied to a plan you want to test. A good objective says what decision must be made and how fast, for example downtime procedures started within 30 minutes.

sections.heading: Participants and ground rules
sections.guidance: List the players by name and role, plus the facilitator and the scribe or evaluator. Include the people who make real decisions on the day: the executive, privacy, clinical leads, the vendor. Set no-fault ground rules so people answer honestly.

sections.heading: Scenario and starting conditions
sections.guidance: Describe the situation at the start in a few sentences: day, time, what people see. Build in Kestrel's real weak points from the data, so the exercise tests what could really go wrong rather than an easy story.

sections.heading: Injects and expected decisions
sections.guidance: Give a timed list of injects (new information the facilitator reveals) and, for each, the decision you expect. The expected decision is what you evaluate against. Escalate through technical, clinical, privacy and executive decisions.

sections.heading: Assumptions under test
sections.guidance: List the assumptions the plans rely on that the exercise should challenge, such as a clean backup or a reachable vendor. Each one should be something the group must confirm or reject during the session.

sections.heading: Evaluation criteria
sections.guidance: For each objective, say what Met looks like and how evaluators will rate it (Met, Partly met, Not met). Without criteria, the debrief turns into opinions.

sections.heading: Hot wash and after-action report
sections.guidance: Plan a short debrief at the end, then a written after-action report with owners and dates. Name the documents the findings will update. Open actions go into the RAID log so they are tracked.

- Document ID: BCN-R3-14
- Title: Tabletop exercise: ransomware encrypts the Clinical Information System
- Owner: Daniel Osei (E-004), Chief Information Security Officer
- Facilitator: Chloe Dubois (E-016), Business Continuity Lead
- Approver: Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), executive sponsor
- Version: 1.0
- Date: 2026-12-07
- Status: Approved for the exercise on Wednesday 2026-12-09, 09:00 to 12:00, KGH

## Purpose and objectives

Test whether Kestrel can keep caring for patients, and recover, when the Clinical Information System (CIS, A-001) is encrypted. Objectives:

1. Start downtime procedures in every emergency department (ED) and inpatient unit within 30 minutes (proposed target).
2. Declare a disaster and name the recovery coordinator within 60 minutes.
3. Contain the attack without destroying evidence.
4. Make the privacy breach assessment and notification decisions under the Health Information Act.
5. Test whether the 4-hour recovery time objective (RTO) and the 8-hour maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) hold against the restore evidence.

## Participants and ground rules

Players: Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), Marcus Bell (E-002), Priya Raman (E-003), Daniel Osei (E-004), Grace Liu (E-005), Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007), Janelle Cardinal (E-008), Kevin Park (E-009), Aisha Mahmoud (E-010), Ahmed Haddad (E-017), Sam Okafor (E-020), and Raj Patel (E-015) for Meridian Clinical Systems. Facilitator: Chloe Dubois. Scribe and evaluator: the Programme Manager.

Ground rules: no fault; answer as you would on the day; use only the plans that exist; the facilitator may pause the clock; nothing said is used in performance reviews.

## Scenario and starting conditions

A Tuesday at 07:00, during the nursing shift change. CIS screens at all four sites show a ransom note, and the CIS servers are encrypted. Starting conditions are Kestrel's real data as of 2026-10-01:

- the last CIS restore test took 13.5 hours against a 4-hour RTO (2025-08-14);
- two privileged accounts have no multi-factor authentication (MFA), one of them the Meridian support account (E-015);
- Clinical Paging (A-014) is past end of support;
- the immutable backup copy check passed on 2026-09-24;
- 121 of 144 staffed beds were occupied on the last census date.

## Injects and expected decisions

| Time | Inject | Expected decision |
|---|---|---|
| 07:00 | Aisha Mahmoud reports the ransom note on KGH emergency screens; the tracking board (A-002) freezes | Start ED downtime procedures; call the service desk |
| 07:15 | Sentinel SOC Services (V-04) sees encryption spreading from a server reached through a vendor remote-support session | Isolate the clinical zone; disable vendor remote access; preserve logs |
| 07:45 | All four sites report the CIS down; pharmacy cannot see orders | Declare a disaster; start the recovery coordinator; open a P1 major incident |
| 09:00 | Kevin Park estimates 13 to 14 hours to restore, based on the last test | Accept the MTD will be passed; decide on ambulance diversion from KGH and extra staff |
| 10:30 | The attacker emails a demand and claims to hold copied patient records | Do not reply; keep the message as evidence; executive decision with legal advice and police |
| 13:00 | Logs confirm records were copied out of the CIS | Risk of harm is present: notify the Commissioner, the Minister responsible under the Act and the affected individuals (section 60.1) |
| 21:00 | CIS restored from the immutable copy; 1 hour of data lost | Back-enter paper records; reconcile medications; return to normal |

## Assumptions under test

- The latest immutable copy is clean and restorable. CT-005 proves the copy exists, not that it restores.
- The Identity Directory (A-007) is not encrypted. If it is, sign-in waits up to 2 more hours.
- Every unit has a current downtime box and downtime report.
- Staff can be reached while paging is unreliable.
- Meridian Clinical Systems can join within 30 minutes at 07:00.
- Sentinel SOC Services can hand over evidence quickly from the United States.

## Evaluation criteria

| Objective | Met when |
|---|---|
| Downtime procedures | Every unit starts within 30 minutes of its inject |
| Declaration | Disaster declared and coordinator named by 08:00 |
| Containment | Isolation chosen without wiping evidence; vendor access cut |
| Privacy | Assessment owner named; notification decision recorded with its reason |
| Recovery targets | Group states the gap between 13.5 h and the 4 h RTO and agrees actions |

Evaluators rate each objective Met, Partly met or Not met, with a note.

## Hot wash and after-action report

A 20-minute hot wash closes the session: what worked, what did not, what surprised you. The scribe records each gap as an action with an owner. The after-action report goes to Daniel Osei by 2026-12-16 and updates the ransomware response playbook, the escalation and breach-notification matrix and the disaster-recovery and downtime plan. Open actions go into the RAID (risks, assumptions, issues and decisions) log.
mistakes: A scenario so easy that every assumption holds. Use Kestrel's real weak points, such as the 13.5-hour restore and the vendor account without multi-factor authentication.
Injects with no expected decision, so evaluators have nothing to rate.
Letting the session become a technical deep-dive or a hunt for someone to blame. It tests decisions, roles and plans.
No after-action report with owners and dates, so the gaps found in the room are forgotten.

## Scope and criteria

Five vendors (V-01 to V-05), the Power BI service, and the software behind the tier 1 systems, including the Clinical Information System (CIS). A supplier is High if it has remote access to clinical systems, holds or reaches Restricted data, processes data outside Canada, or its last independent assurance report (for example a SOC 2 Type 2 report or an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate) is missing or more than 12 months old.

## Supplier ratings

| Vendor | Findings | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| V-01 Meridian Clinical Systems (CIS software and remote support) | Remote access; support account E-015 is privileged, has no multi-factor authentication (MFA) and no end date; CIS patch SEC-012 past due; assurance 2026-03-31 | High |
| V-02 NorthArc Cloud (hosting and backup) | Remote access (E-039, MFA on); hosts A-011, A-012, A-013 and A-015, so one outage hits backups, service desk, email and human resources (HR) together; assurance 2026-05-15 | High |

| V-05 Lumen Analytics Partners (Power BI consulting) | Remote access; assurance 2025-06-30 (458 days old); contract ended 2026-11-30 | High by the assurance rule until removal of its access is confirmed |
| Power BI service (A-009) | Vendor hosted, but its provider is not in the vendor register | To be rated |

## Software risks

| System | Issue | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| A-014 Clinical Paging and Secure Messaging | End of support 2026-06-30; SEC-015 (High) 43 days past due on 2026-10-01 | High: unsupported tier 1 system |

## Privacy and data location

V-04 processes Kestrel's security logs in the United States. Logs that contain patient identifiers are health information under the Health Information Act. - notice to Kestrel within 24 hours of any security incident touching Kestrel data, so Kestrel can meet its own breach duties;
- data location, named subcontractors, and return or destruction of data at exit;
- a current independent assurance report every year, and Kestrel's right to audit;
- named support accounts with MFA, an end date and access only when approved;
- for software vendors: a secure development process, a software bill of materials (SBOM), Critical fixes within 7 days of release, and 12 months' notice of end of support;
- awareness training for every vendor and agency worker before access.

| Privacy review and contract safeguards for V-04, or move log processing to Canada | Priya Raman (E-003) | 2027-01-29 |
| Confirm V-05 access to the Beacon workspace was removed at contract end | Tomás Rivera (E-006) | 2026-12-11 |
| Confirm A-014 is isolated in its own network zone with admin access limited, and approve a replacement plan | Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), Ahmed Haddad (E-017) | 2027-03-31 |

## Approval and review

Approved by Marcus Bell on 2026-12-08 on the advice of Daniel Osei and Priya Raman. High suppliers are reviewed every 6 months, others every year, and every supplier before a renewal or new access. Residual supplier risks go to the residual risk register.
mistakes: Rating suppliers by contract value instead of by access, data and how much recovery depends on them.
Treating data in Canada as a legal requirement. It is Kestrel contract and policy; the Health Information Act requires safeguards for health information stored or used outside Alberta.
Looking only at the company and not its people: support accounts without MFA or end dates are the most common supplier weakness.
Assessing once at signing and never again, so expired assurance reports and ended contracts go unnoticed.

sections.heading: Summary and scope

items.modelDocument:
- Document ID: BCN-R3-16
- Title: Post-incident review: SEC-004, ransomware precursor on the Virtual Desktop Service
- Owner: Daniel Osei (E-004), Chief Information Security Officer
- Prepared by: Sam Okafor (E-020), Security Analyst and security operations centre (SOC) liaison
- Approver: Marcus Bell (E-002), Chief Information Officer (CIO)
- Version: 1.0
- Date: 2026-12-14
- Status: Approved
- Evidence: khn_security_events.csv, khn_assets.csv and khn_controls.csv, as of 2026-10-01

## Summary and scope

On Tuesday 2026-08-11 at 02:20, activity that comes before a ransomware attack started on the Virtual Desktop Service (A-008), the tier 1 service clinicians use to reach the Clinical Information System (CIS) from shared workstations. It was detected 45 minutes later and contained 2 hours 40 minutes after detection, but normal service did not return until 2026-08-13 at 18:30. This review is blameless: it asks what in Kestrel's systems and processes allowed this, not who made a mistake. It is four months late because Beacon scheduled it in Release 3; future reviews are held within 10 working days (proposed).

## Timeline

| Time | Event | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-07-14 13:05 | SEC-002, Medium malware on A-008 | khn_security_events.csv |
| 2026-08-11 02:20 | SEC-004 activity starts | occurred_at |
| 2026-08-11 03:05 | Detected | detected_at |
| 2026-08-11 03:20 | Record opened in the IT Service Management Platform (A-011) | opened_at |
| 2026-08-11 05:45 | Contained | contained_at |
| 2026-08-12 06:00 | SEC-011, Critical remote code execution weakness, found on A-008 | SEC-011 |
| 2026-08-13 18:30 | Normal service restored | recovered_at |
| 2026-09-09 11:00 | SEC-008, Medium malware on A-008 | SEC-008 |

## Response performance

MTTD, MTTC and MTTR are the mean times to detect, contain and recover over Q3 (1 July to 30 September 2026) incidents with a valid time sequence: 9 incidents, 8 of them recovered for MTTR.

| Measure | SEC-004 | Q3 average, valid incidents | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Time to detect | 0.75 h | 25.29 h (MTTD) | None set |
| Detection to containment | 2.67 h | 1.93 h (MTTC) | None set |
| Detection to normal service | 63.42 h | 28.33 h (MTTR) | 4 h (RTO of A-008) |

Detection was fast and containment near the average. Recovery failed: 63.42 hours against a 4-hour recovery time objective (RTO).

## Causes and contributing conditions

Why did recovery take 63.4 hours?

1. There was no tested way to rebuild the service: khn_controls.csv holds no restore test for A-008.
2. Why not? Restore tests existed only for A-001 and A-007 (A-005's never ran), and before Release 3 there was no business impact analysis to say which systems needed one.
3. Why was the service exposed? Malware reached A-008 three times in Q3 (SEC-002, SEC-004, SEC-008), but no problem record linked them, so the cause was never removed.
4. A Critical weakness (SEC-011) sat on A-008 and was found only during recovery.

The entry route is not established in the record. It stays open as problem PRB-01 rather than being guessed.

## Privacy and notification check

The SEC-004 record has no field for a privacy breach assessment, so the review cannot show one was made. Under section 60.1 of the Health Information Act, where there is a risk of harm to an individual as a result of the loss of, or unauthorized access to or disclosure of, health information, Kestrel must notify the Information and Privacy Commissioner, the Minister responsible under the Act and the affected individuals. Priya Raman (E-003) completes and files the assessment for SEC-004.

## Corrective actions

| ID | Action | Owner | Due | Measure |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PIR-1 | Find and remove the entry route under problem PRB-01 (repeat malware on A-008; problem owner Ahmed Haddad, E-017) | Sam Okafor (E-020) | 2027-01-15 | Cause recorded and removed |
| PIR-2 | Write and test an A-008 rebuild procedure against its 4-hour RTO | Ahmed Haddad (E-017) | 2027-02-26 | Timed test within 4 h |
| PIR-3 | Scan tier 1 systems for Critical weaknesses every week (proposed) | Sam Okafor (E-020) | 2027-01-15 | Weekly scan report |
| PIR-4 | Add a mandatory privacy assessment field to every security incident; file SEC-004's | Priya Raman (E-003) | 2027-01-15 | Field live; assessment filed |
| PIR-5 | Hold post-incident reviews within 10 working days | Daniel Osei (E-004) | 2027-01-15 | Next review on time |

## Follow-up and sign-off

Actions are tracked in the RAID (risks, assumptions, issues and decisions) log and reviewed at the monthly security operations meeting until closed. The slow recovery of A-008 goes to the residual risk register as RR-05. Approved by Marcus Bell on 2026-12-14.
mistakes: Naming a person as the root cause. Keep asking why until you reach something in the system that Kestrel can change.
Stopping at containment. SEC-004 was contained in 2 hours 40 minutes but took 63.4 hours to restore, and that is where the lesson is.
Guessing the entry route to finish the story. Record unknowns as open problems with an owner.
Skipping the privacy check because the incident looked purely technical.

items.purpose: The major-incident service restoration review looks at a major incident from the service consumer's side: how fast service came back, how the incident was handled and communicated, which workarounds existed, and what should improve. You build it in week 12, day 5, with the post-incident review, using the same incident, SEC-004; in the programme it is held the day after that review (task 26, 2026-12-15). Its actions go to the continual-improvement register. ITIL incident management, problem management and continual improvement.

sections.heading: Incident and service impact
sections.guidance: Name the service, its tier and recovery time objective (RTO), its owner and custodian, the consumers affected and the incident record. Describe impact the way consumers felt it. Clinicians reach the Clinical Information System (CIS) through this service, so for them losing it is like losing the CIS.

sections.guidance: Show each stage of restoration in hours and minutes against the RTO and the period averages, then say where the time went. Most of SEC-004's time was spent after containment, which points at rebuilding, not at stopping the attack.

sections.heading: Service desk handling and communication

- Document ID: BCN-R3-17
- Title: Major-incident service restoration review: SEC-004, Virtual Desktop Service
- Owner: Grace Liu (E-005), IT Service Desk Manager
- Co-owner: Daniel Osei (E-004), Chief Information Security Officer
- Approver: Marcus Bell (E-002), Chief Information Officer (CIO)
- Version: 1.0
- Date: 2026-12-15
- Status: Approved

## Incident and service impact

Service: Virtual Desktop Service (A-008), tier 1, recovery time objective (RTO) 4 h, business owner Marcus Bell, custodian Ahmed Haddad (E-017). Consumers: clinicians at all four sites who reach the Clinical Information System (CIS) from shared workstations, so for them losing this service feels like losing the CIS. Incident: SEC-004, Critical, ransomware precursor, detected 2026-08-11 03:05, normal service 2026-08-13 18:30.

## Restoration against targets

| Stage | SEC-004 | Comparison |
|---|---|---|
| Detection to record opened | 15 min | |
| Detection to containment | 2 h 40 min | Q3 (July to September 2026) mean time to contain 1.93 h |
| Containment to normal service | 60 h 45 min | |
| Detection to normal service | 63 h 25 min | RTO 4 h; Q3 mean time to recover 28.33 h |

Restoration took almost 16 times the RTO, and most of it came after containment. The gap is in rebuilding and checking the service, not in stopping the attack.

## Service desk handling and communication

- khn_service_desk.csv has no P1 ticket from 2026-08-11 to 2026-08-13; the four P1 tickets in Q3 are all later. No major incident was raised in the service desk record.
- Five incident tickets in the Virtual desktop or CIS issue categories were opened during the outage (SD-10029, SD-10030, SD-10036, SD-10037, SD-10049), the highest at P2. None is linked to SEC-004, so the review cannot tell which ones it caused.
- The incident record holds no times for messages to clinicians, so time to first notice cannot be measured.

## Workarounds

Before Release 3, Kestrel had no tested downtime procedure for clinicians who lose their virtual desktop. That gap is why Release 3 exists. The disaster-recovery and downtime plan now gives one (paper records and the unit downtime report workstation). It must also be written as a known error article, with the symptom, the workaround and who may use it, so the service desk can give it on the first call.

## Continual improvement model

Kestrel uses the seven questions of the ITIL 4 continual improvement model, which ITIL Version 5 refines.

| Question | Answer for the Virtual Desktop Service |
|---|---|
| What is the vision? | Clinicians can always reach patient records, even during a cyber attack |
| Where are we now? | 63.4 h to restore against a 4-hour RTO; malware on A-008 three times in Q3; no restore test on file |
| Where do we want to be? | Restored within 4 h, proven by a timed test, by 2027-02-26 |
| How do we get there? | Actions MIR-1 to MIR-5 |
| Take action | Owners deliver them through the continual-improvement register |
| Did we get there? | Checked at the A-008 restore test and at the 2027-03-17 benefits review |
| How do we keep the momentum going? | Quarterly service review of restore results and repeat incidents |

Dimensions touched: Organizations and People (no major incident raised), Information and Technology (no rebuild procedure), Partners and Suppliers (evidence from Sentinel SOC Services, V-04), Value Streams and Processes (security and service desk records not linked).

## Improvement actions

| ID | Action | Lifecycle stage | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MIR-1 | Raise a P1 major incident for every Critical security incident on a tier 1 service | Support | Grace Liu (E-005) | 2027-01-15 |
| MIR-2 | Link every related ticket to the major incident record | Support | Grace Liu (E-005) | 2027-01-15 |
| MIR-3 | Publish a known error and workaround article for loss of A-008 | Support | Ahmed Haddad (E-017) | 2027-01-29 |
| MIR-4 | Log every message to clinicians with a time; first notice within 15 minutes (proposed) | Support | Grace Liu (E-005) | 2027-01-29 |
| MIR-5 | Timed rebuild procedure for A-008 (shared with PIR-2) | Operate | Ahmed Haddad (E-017) | 2027-02-26 |

## Approval

Approved by Marcus Bell on 2026-12-15. MIR-1 to MIR-5 are entered in the continual-improvement register and reviewed monthly by Grace Liu at the service review. Problem PRB-01 (repeat malware on A-008, opened in the incident and problem management workflow and worked by PIR-1) stays with problem management until its cause is removed.
mistakes: Repeating the technical post-incident review instead of judging the service from the consumer's side: restoration, communication and workarounds.
Closing the problem when the incident closes. Three malware incidents on one service in a quarter need problem management.
Using ITIL 4 value chain activities as if they were current terms. Name the Version 5 lifecycle stages, such as Operate and Support.
Improvement actions with no measure or date, so nobody can answer Did we get there?

items.purpose: The residual risk register lists the risks that remain after Beacon's controls are in place, each with an owner, a residual rating, an acceptance decision by someone with the authority to make it, the conditions of acceptance and an expiry date. Daniel Osei (E-004) maintains it as risk acceptance advisor; each owner proposes a decision, and Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001) and Marcus Bell (E-002) accept within their authority. You build it in week 13, day 1, while reviewing the eight CISSP domains through Beacon; it is dated 2026-12-16, attached to the programme closure report, and then reviewed every quarter. CISSP Security and Risk Management, across all eight domains.

sections.heading: Scope and acceptance rules
sections.guidance: Define residual risk, the rating scale and who may accept each rating. Say that every accepted risk has conditions and an expiry date, and that a risk with no owner cannot be accepted. Label the authority levels as agreed.

sections.heading: Residual risks
sections.guidance: One row per risk: ID (with the RAID ID it came from), a plain statement with the evidence, the main CISSP domain, the owner, the rating and the decision. Covering all eight domains shows you looked across the whole programme, not only at the loudest risk.

sections.heading: Acceptance conditions
sections.guidance: For each High risk, say what must stay true for the acceptance to hold and what evidence will lower the rating. A rating should fall only on evidence that a control works, never because work was done.

sections.heading: Programme risks closed or transferred

sections.heading: Review and escalation

sections.heading: Sign-off
sections.guidance: Record who accepted which risks and in what role, and any risk returned without acceptance. The approver's authority must match the rating.

## Scope and acceptance rules

Residual risk is the risk left after controls. Ratings: Low, Medium, High, Very high. Acceptance authority (agreed): Low by the risk owner; Medium by the Chief Information Officer (CIO, E-002); High by the executive sponsor (E-001) on the CISO's advice; Very high cannot be accepted and must be treated. Every acceptance has conditions and an expiry date. A risk with no owner cannot be accepted.

| RR-02 | Clinical Paging (A-014) unsupported since 2026-06-30; SEC-015 open | Asset Security | E-001 | High | Accepted by E-001 to 2027-03-31 |

| RR-05 | Virtual Desktop Service (A-008) took 63.4 h to restore after SEC-004; no restore test | Security Operations | E-002 | High | Accepted by E-001 to 2027-02-26 |

## Acceptance conditions

items.purpose: The programme closure report formally closes Project Beacon. Residual risk register (BCN-R3-18): the sponsor accepted three High risks with conditions: CIS restore (RR-01), unsupported Clinical Paging (RR-02) and Virtual Desktop Service recovery (RR-05). RR-03, the Pharmacy System with no business owner, was returned to the sponsor to name one. SEC-004 review actions (PIR-1 to PIR-5, MIR-1 to MIR-5) stay with their owners.

## Lessons learned

1. Agree cleaning rules before anyone sees a number: 480 visit rows became 474 valid visits by stated rules, which made Release 1 trusted.
2. Ask what is the least information needed: CR-01 found a better answer than yes or no.
3. Put statutory holidays in the calendar: the schedule had none, so Thanksgiving (2026-10-12) and Remembrance Day (2026-11-11) were not planned for.
4. Settle cross-team timing early: a facilitated session and an agreed change window ended the week 9 gateway firewall dispute between Tomás Rivera and Ahmed Haddad.
5. A backup never restored is not a recovery plan: two failed CIS tests and a 63.4-hour Virtual Desktop recovery made the case for Release 3.
